dietEvidence.body: The dental batteries and jaw apparatus are consistent with herbivory. No gut contents are known, and the plants eaten are not preserved.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A hadrosaurid with a hatchet-shaped crest and a hollow nasal passage. The crest shape varies between species and growth stages.
summary: A hadrosaurid with a hatchet-shaped crest and a hollow nasal passage. The crest shape varies between species and growth stages.

discovery.body: Named by William Parks in 1923 from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta. Parks based the species on two skulls, CMN 351 and CMN 2869; Charles Gilmore selected CMN 2869 as the type in 1924. The crest is hatchet-shaped and hollow.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Several skulls and partial skeletons from Alberta.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Dinosaur Park Formation, Alberta records the species in the Late Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈77–75 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The crest is tall and hatchet-shaped, and the skull is long with a broad, toothless beak.

behaviour.body: Herbivory is inferred from the dental batteries. The crest may have functioned in display or vocalisation, but social behaviour and sound production are inferred from anatomy, not observed.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from several skulls and partial skeletons from Alberta. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The crest and internal nasal passages are well documented, but the soft tissues that would have produced sound are not preserved. The type history is complicated, and species-level growth variation remains debated.
